findings.where: the composer sheet at the foot of the frame, the grey line reading "↵ answering leaving now. dont cut the end … ×" (y≈2490 of 3120) — and, by absence, every other artifact
findings.what: The only reply anywhere in the capture is one being typed: no thread row in any of the fifteen artifacts shows a sent or received message tied to the message it answers, and the only reply-shaped field in any per-scene report is `view.replying_to` (the composer's pending target, 0001M2ZNX8AF4811Y2F7FNAGMG here) — `grep -o '"repl[a-z_]*"' evidence/logs/*.report.json` returns `replying_to` six times and nothing else, and I read every sheet in 50 frames sampled evenly across the 300 frames of 11_chat_scroll.mp4 (rows ~5000–5060 of 8075, Wed 22 Apr 17:20 to Mon 27 Apr 16:25) without finding one quoted parent.
findings.why: The row names replies among the capabilities that must be present and dependable; a reply that arrives with no visible tie to what it answers is exactly the message a couple loses the thread of, and answering the third message up is a daily Instagram DM action.

findings.where: `problems` in logs/11_chat_scroll.json and logs/07_feeling_landing.json, against `reports[0].sync` in the same two files
findings.what: Two of the fifteen scenes recorded the message-receive poll being refused: `http: 401 GET http://127.0.0.1:8480/v1/events?after=14075&wait=20` (11_chat_scroll) and `...after=14079&wait=20` (07_feeling_landing), each with a matching console 401. In 07 the refusal is mid-run — cursor 14079 with the scene ending at 14087, so eight further events arrived after it — yet the same file's sync block reads `faults: 0`, `last_error: null`, `state: "connected"`, `rounds: 317`. The app's own link record carries no trace of the failure it just had.
findings.why: That poll is how the phone learns a message exists. If it can be refused while the link still reports itself connected — the same state 05_settings.png prints to the person as "LINK connected · http://127.0.0.1:8480" — then no delivery or read marker on the glass can be trusted, and silence would be indistinguishable from being ignored. I cannot tell from the evidence whether the cause is the app or a re-pair by the capture; what is certain either way is that the app did not notice.

findings.what: The only frame-cost measurement in the set says the app never once drew a frame in under 16 ms: `over_16ms` is 778 of 778, and I re-derived the distribution — build_ms p50 4, p90 700, p95 783, p99 918, max 1055; total_ms p50 113, p95 896; zero frames at or under 33 ms. 179 of the 778 frames spend over 100 ms in build alone, spaced every three to five frames and spread evenly across all twenty segments of the scene (8 or 9 per 38-frame segment throughout).
findings.why: "No scroll jank against the year-deep seeded history" is not shown by the clip, because the clip cannot show it: the clock is driven, so each of 11_chat_scroll.mp4's 300 frames is grabbed after the build finishes, and the fling log's asked==moved measures the list's arithmetic rather than its speed. The one number that bears on cost does not support the claim. The raster half of it is environmental (p50 104 ms is software rasterisation with no GPU), but build p50 on the same CPU is 4 ms, so a 200x spread in build is not the machine being slow.

findings.what: The transport reads "0:00 / 0:03" with the playhead at the left stop, and logs/14_media_viewer.report.json puts it at `position_ms: 32` of `duration_ms: 2500` with `playing: true`. There is no clip of the viewer, so no artifact in the set shows a video advancing one frame. (32 ms is consistent with correct playback under a driven clock — the scene's `driven_ms` is 176 — so this is an evidence gap, not a demonstrated stall.)
findings.why: Video is one of the enumerated capabilities and motion is the whole of it; the set proves the file decoded and the transport is wired, and nothing more.

findings.what: First launch with the year importing takes 8.9–10.0 seconds — `load.ms` 9935 (13_messenger_states), 9733 (08_state_propagating), 8865 (01_pulse), 8099 (dusk_pulse), 7347 (reception) on `store: fresh`; a phone that already has it takes 2078–2495 ms across the nine `store: kept` scenes. No artifact shows what is on the screen during either.
findings.why: "No spinner that outstays its welcome" cannot be checked against a picture anywhere in the set, and a ten-second first launch is the interval in which somebody opens the app that opens instantly instead.

findings.what: Seven full throws over 300 frames move 8455 logical pixels in total, against a scroll extent the same log reports between 274,389 and 681,687 — so one hard fling covers 1.2 to 3.1 per cent of the thread. No frame of the clip shows a scrollbar, a date rail, or a jump-to-latest control; the only way back to now that the evidence supports is leaving the tab and returning, since 13 and 12 both open at the end (`scroll.first` 8068 of 8075, 8063 of 8069).
findings.why: Looking something up and then getting back to the newest message is a daily action in an 8,075-row thread, and the person is given neither a control nor any sense of where they are.

findings.where: the fifth sheet, "sending you the roster", y≈1700–1870 of 3120
findings.what: The far side refused with a specific reason — "this phone is on an older version and cannot read that" (scenes/13_messenger_states.json step 7, echoed in logs/13_messenger_states.json `far`) — and the glass shows only "it would not go ✕" over "send it again". The reason never reaches the person.
findings.why: The one action offered is the wrong one for the cause that was actually given, and there is no way to tell a failure that will clear on a retry from one that will not.

findings.where: the lower-right corner of the top sheet, the reaction at roughly x=1150–1216, y=560–640
findings.what: The pink reaction and its cast shadow are cut by a hard vertical edge at x≈1216, well to the right of the sheet's torn edge: the object's right twist is sliced flat. It is the only reaction on the glass in that frame, and the only other one in the set (0001M59VY0YA13H9M86HTA6XNP in 13_messenger_states.report.json) sits on the row clipped to a blank 56-pixel sliver at the top of the scroll region (y=282–338), so it is not visible at all.
findings.why: Reactions are an enumerated capability and the set contains exactly two: one half-drawn, one invisible.

findings.what: No artifact shows two screens at once, so delivery and read markers are never seen changing on the sending phone as the other phone receives and reads. The stated reason is measured rather than asserted — no /dev/kvm, adbd answering after 113 minutes with no framework behind it, no GTK for a desktop stand-in — which I judge a reason and not an excuse.
findings.why: It leaves the two-sided half of "delivery and read state" resting on 08_state_propagating.mp4, which is one screen with the far side scripted, and on evidence/reliability.json, which is the build's own report of itself.

what_is_working: Every capability the row names except replies is visible somewhere in the set: text (02_chat.png, 13_messenger_states.png), photos inline in the thread (11_chat_scroll.mp4 frame 61) and as search thumbnails (12_search.png), video (14_media_viewer.png), a voice note with a waveform, a 0:26 duration and a play control (02_chat.png), a reaction (02_chat.png), sending/sent/refused on one screen and read on another (13_messenger_states.png: sent 3, "it would not go" 1, "going" 1; 02_chat.png: read 3), typing as "noor writing…" (11 and 13), "· edited ↵" beside the state (13), a deletion left as the stub "took this back" (13), search over 8,069 rows with fifteen facets and the query highlighted in each hit (12), a media gallery with three lenses and both photo and voice rows (04_moments.png), and the viewer itself (14).

Read state is applied correctly by author: in 02_chat.png the three outgoing sheets carry "read ✓✓" and the four incoming ones carry no state at all, matching logs/02_chat.report.json (delivery: 4 entries all read, states_on_the_glass read: 3, the fourth off-screen).

Ordering holds over the dense scroll. I read every sheet in 50 frames sampled evenly across 11_chat_scroll.mp4 and the timestamps run strictly forward — Wed 22 Apr 17:20, Thu 23 Apr, Fri 24 Apr, Sat 25 Apr, Sun 26 Apr, Mon 27 Apr 16:25 — with no repeat, no inversion and no blank or placeholder row anywhere in the 300 frames.

I re-extracted all five clips with ffmpeg and re-ran the briefing's three-term held-frame test myself: 0 held frames and 0 byte-identical repeats in 06 (310 frames), 07 (421), 08 (639), 11 (300) and 15 (376). My mean-change figures — 2.969, 4.147, 3.462, 19.280, 4.754 — match frames.json to three decimals, so its numbers check out rather than having to be trusted.

The fling is exact: all 300 entries of logs/11_chat_scroll.fling.json have `asked` equal to `moved` to three decimals (max |asked-moved| = 0.0 over the whole log), no frame moved less than a third of a logical pixel, and the per-frame decay is smooth within each of the seven throws.

Drafts survive everything the capture does to them: the composer holds "the second one, then" in every one of the 300 frames of 11_chat_scroll.mp4 and in 06, 07 and 13, across region changes, an attach menu, a pending reply and a send in flight.

Failure is legible and recoverable rather than silent: "it would not go ✕" with "send it again" underneath, and the refused item kept rather than dropped (logs/13_messenger_states.report.json: refused_in_the_outbox 1, pending 2, events 14074 against cursor 14072).

Notification actually reaches a banner through a service worker, with the sender named and the content withheld ("noor / wrote something", "noor / is holding something out" in crops/reception.png and crops/reception_replaced.png), tagged so a new one replaces the old rather than stacking, and governed by per-type preferences and quiet hours 23:00–07:00 that are editable on 05_settings.png. logs/reception.json is candid that this is Chromium on a Linux display and not an iPhone banner.

evidence/reliability.json's twenty-two capability checks all pass over 177 events on both sides with 0 duplicates, the same order on both sides, monotonic sequence, 26 events queued offline and all delivered on reconnect, seq 1..175 gapless after the gap, a kill mid-send that did not duplicate, a draft and pairing intact across a process restart, and a stale pairing that says "the other phone does not know this pairing" instead of polling with a forgotten key.
verdict: This is a real messenger, not a mock-up of one, and most of the row is genuinely met: twelve of the thirteen named capabilities are visible on the glass, read state is applied to the right author's sheets, five days of dense thread scroll past in strict chronological order with no blank row and no held or duplicated frame in any of the five clips, the fling moved exactly what it was asked to move on all three hundred frames, the draft survives every region change and send in the capture, and a failed send says so and offers a retry instead of vanishing. What holds the row below its floor is that replies — named in the row alongside reactions and read state — exist in the evidence only as something being typed: 13_messenger_states.png photographs a reply in the composer with its target quoted, and then no artifact anywhere shows a reply that has landed, no thread row is drawn as an answer to another, and no per-scene report has a field for one. That is the blocking finding, and it is the cheapest to settle: photograph a delivered reply beside its parent, or build the row that draws it. Behind it sits the finding I would fix second — two of fifteen scenes recorded the event-receive poll being refused with 401 while the app's own link record for the same run reads faults 0, last_error null, connected — because a link that cannot see its own failures is what turns a missing message into a fight. Third is that the only frame-cost measurement in the set says no frame was ever drawn in under 16 ms and that a quarter of builds cost over 100 ms, which the driven-clock clip cannot corroborate or refute either way. The rest are edges: a ten-second first launch with no picture of what is on screen during it, an 8,075-row thread with no way back to now, a refusal whose stated reason never reaches the person, and two reactions in the whole set of which one is sliced by a clip rectangle and the other is scrolled to an invisible sliver.

not_worth_opening.why: I opened the scene logs themselves, which embed the same report block, and read the report files directly for the six messenger scenes (02, 11, 12, 13, 14 and 08 via its scene log). Re-opening the standalone copies for the Pulse, Us, Moments, Settings, first-run, feeling and setup scenes would have added nothing my row turns on.

22,998 bytes of per-pattern vibration strings. Haptics are the feeling row's business, not messenger reliability; I read haptics.check.json and the haptics strip instead to confirm the patterns exist and are distinct.
68,733 bytes of surface measurements for paper, desk and objects — the material-truth row. Nothing in it bears on whether a message arrives, orders correctly or shows the right state.

The reception scene is explicitly not one of the artifacts. I read logs/reception.json for what it recorded and looked at three of its five crops; the step log and region report would only have told me how the picture was taken.

Two more frames of the same Chromium notification sequence I already read in logs/reception.json and saw in reception.png, reception_open.png and reception_replaced.png. The permission-grant and state-declared variants would not change what I can say about message delivery.
I read the scene scripts for the six scenes my findings rest on, so I could tell a fault in the app from a fault in the framing. For the others I read the step log, which records what actually ran.

My row is read from the artifacts. WHY_MISSING.json and MANIFEST.json cite docs/PHONES.md for the Android attempts; I judged the reason on the measurements quoted in the evidence itself (no /dev/kvm, adbd at 113 minutes, no GTK) rather than on the account.
